question: Where do traditional medicines mostly come from?
explanation: You'll find that traditional healing systems rely heavily on what is freely available around them—using gifts from the plant kingdom, animal parts, and natural minerals. Great job thinking about your roots! [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why should you as a nurse always ask your patients if they use traditional herbs or local remedies?

options.A: To report illegal practitioners to the local authorities
options.B: To calculate the exact economic cost of local healthcare
options.C: To prevent dangerous interactions with hospital medications
options.D: To replace all expensive hospital drugs with free herbs

explanation: Patients often mix local herbs with hospital drugs without mentioning it. Checking for this helps keep them safe from unexpected drug reactions. You're learning to think like a safe, caring nurse! [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h1)

question: In many rural Nigerian communities, who is usually the very first person consulted when someone falls ill?
explanation: Because traditional healers and birth attendants are trusted and easy to reach in rural areas, people often visit them first before coming to a modern clinic. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h2)

question: Many Nigerians view illness through both physical and spiritual lenses. How does this affect how they seek healthcare?

options.A: It completely stops people from ever visiting modern health clinics
options.B: It ensures that every disease is cured instantly without medication
options.C: It forces the government to ban all imported pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: It leads many patients to combine traditional healing with orthodox medicine

explanation: When people believe an illness has both physical and spiritual causes, it's very natural for them to seek help from both traditional healers and medical doctors to cover all bases! [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which part of a plant is most commonly used in traditional remedies?
explanation: Leaves are a nurse's and healer's best friend! They are abundant, easy to gather, and grow back quickly without killing the plant. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h3)

question: What do plant 'secondary metabolites' mainly do for the plant and for medicine?

options.C: Storing plain water during heavy droughts
options.D: Providing basic structural cellulose for the stem

explanation: Plants make special chemicals like alkaloids to protect themselves from pests. Luckily for us, these exact same natural chemicals often have healing powers in humans! [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is a major health risk linked to certain traditional mineral-based treatments?
explanation: Unpurified local mineral remedies can sometimes contain dangerous heavy metals like lead or mercury. It is a great reminder why safety checks matter in patient care. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h4)

question: How are animal fats and oils usually used in traditional medicine?

options.A: As intravenous substitutes for blood plasma
options.B: As sterile eye drops for acute glaucoma
options.C: As primary replacements for oral antibiotics
options.D: As bases for topical balms and ointments

explanation: Animal fats make a nice, greasy base that helps carry healing ingredients and keeps them sticking to the skin to soothe pain or swelling. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is the main difference between making an infusion and making a decoction?

options.A: Decoctions are always applied topically, while infusions are inhaled
options.B: Infusions use alcohol exclusively, while decoctions use only palm oil
options.C: Decoctions involve boiling hard parts, while infusions soak softer parts
options.D: Infusions require high-pressure machinery, unlike simple decoctions

explanation: Think of it like tea: tough roots and bark need a good long boil (decoction) to release their goodness, while soft leaves just need a gentle soak (infusion). [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h5)

question: A patient comes to the clinic with severe belly pain and rectal bleeding after using a local herbal enema. What is the biggest nursing concern here?

options.A: Severe allergic rhinitis and upper airway swelling
options.B: Sudden complete obstruction of the upper esophagus
options.C: Trauma to the rectal mucosa and systemic toxicity

explanation: Harsh local enemas can easily tear the delicate lining of the rectum and quickly push strong, unmeasured chemicals straight into the bloodstream. Ouch! Patient safety is key here. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why is it much harder to get an exact, consistent dose from herbal medicines compared to factory-made tablets?

options.A: Government regulations strictly forbid the weighing of plant roots
options.B: Active ingredient levels vary based on soil, weather, and plant maturity
options.C: Herbal remedies lose all chemical potency within two hours of harvest
options.D: Traditional healers refuse to use measuring spoons and cups

explanation: Mother Nature doesn't use a laboratory scale! Plants grow differently depending on the soil and weather, meaning the strength of the active ingredients changes from one harvest to the next. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h6)

question: In healthcare, what does the term 'pharmacovigilance' mean?

options.A: Monitoring and studying adverse drug reactions and safety issues
options.B: Manufacturing synthetic drugs in sterile laboratory environments
options.C: Setting international market prices for essential pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: Inspecting local pharmacies for expired prescription medications

explanation: Pharmacovigilance simply means keeping a watchful eye on medications to catch, study, and prevent any harmful side effects. You're building great clinical vocabulary! [learn more](GNS125_U2_T2#GNS125_U2_T2_h6)
